extracted_by: hand, T-0311 — the Democrat read, February 1834
note: Vol. I No. 11. The month's heaviest issue for the town itself: the Trustees of the Town of Chicago advertise for proposals to repair BOTH river bridges and specify them timber by timber; the Chicago Temperance Society holds its annual meeting inside the Presbyterian Church and elects a board; the Eagle Hotel is named as Steele's and is twice used as the town's public room; and the building formerly occupied as the Meeting-House, opposite the North Branch bridge, is put up at auction. The issue also reprints the post office's list of letters for 1 January 1834 — the THIRD printing of that one list, and much the best witness to it.

claims.notes: THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IS A ROOM THE TOWN MEETS IN, and this is the claim that shows it working. On the evening of Thursday 30 January 1834 the Chicago Temperance Society held its annual meeting there before what the paper calls 'so large an assem[bly] of the respectable and intelligent citizens [of C]hicago' — an audience, a read address and an election, not a service. For a reconstruction that has to decide how big the church's interior is and whether it is furnished for a crowd, a documented secular assembly inside it is worth more than another exterior view. The officers are the town's professional men — two physicians as president and vice-president, Philo Carpenter as secretary — and TWO OF THE SEVEN COMMITTEE MEN ARE GARRISON OFFICERS, Capt. D. Wilcox and Lieut. J. L. Thompson, both 'U. S. A.', which puts Fort Dearborn inside the town's civil life a second time in as many months (T-0310 c001 and c002 put a wedding and an auction inside the fort). The left-hand sliver of the segmenter column carries the Eagle Hotel notice woven through these lines, so the claim is interleaved and only the lines naming the society's business are quoted.

claims.notes: THE EAGLE HOTEL IS STEELE'S, and that parenthesis is the whole value of the claim. The paper names the house and then names its keeper in the same breath, because readers were expected to know it by the man rather than by the sign — which is how a tavern stand is identified on the ground and how this project's records have to carry it (T-0076, buildings named for their people). The Eagle is also doing public work: this notice and the Cook county call twelve lines below (claim c004) both summon the town into it, and the auction of claim c006 is cried there two days later. A house used three times in one issue as the town's public room is a house with a room big enough to hold one. NO PLACEMENT IS GIVEN and none is invented; the paper never says which street the Eagle stands on.

claims.notes: A NAMED BUILDING WITH A PLACEMENT THE MODEL CAN USE: 'the Building formerly occupied as the Meeting-House, opposite the bridge over the North Branch of the Chicago river.' Three facts fall out of one sentence. It is a building that SURVIVES its use — a meeting-house in the past tense, still standing and saleable in February 1834, so a structure of that footprint stands at that spot at the scene date unless something later says otherwise. It is placed by the town's own landmark, the North Branch bridge, and 'opposite' is the paper's word, not a reading. And it is sold at the Eagle Hotel with two platted lots — West half of Lot 3 in Block 44, and Lot 7 in Block 8 — which are block-and-lot references this project can resolve against the plat. THE BUILDING'S OWN SIDE OF THE RIVER IS NOT STATED and is not inferred: 'opposite the bridge' fixes it against the crossing, not against a bank, and the difference is a hundred feet of ground. Cried by J. Bates jr, the same auctioneer who sold soldier's bread inside Fort Dearborn three weeks earlier (T-0310, 1834-01-14 c002).

claims.notes: THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE PASSAGE IN THE MONTH, and possibly in the corpus so far, because it is a BILL OF MATERIALS FOR BOTH CHICAGO BRIDGES written by the body that owned them. Everything dimensioned here is dimensioned in the paper's own words: braces of OAK TIMBER 6 INCHES SQUARE, two complete sets to each bridge; OAK RAILING 8 BY 4 INCHES for both bridges; OAK STANDARDS for the railing 4 FEET HIGH; decking of OAK PLANK 2 INCHES thick, pinned down with OAK PINS 1 1-2 INCHES IN DIAMETER AND 2 FEET IN LENGTH; the railing spiked or pinned. The project has been drawing both bridges from engravings and from general practice; this is a documented specification, and it is dated — 4 January 1834, work to be paid for on 15 August 1834 — so it describes the bridges as they stood eighteen months before the scene date and as they were about to be repaired, not as they were first built. TWO THINGS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT READ. The standards' spacing is lost at the column edge ('aby / art, 4 fect high') and is supplied as [4 feet] apart only inside brackets, because a railing post spacing is exactly the sort of number a reconstruction would later cite as documented. And 'a new bent to the [so]uth bridge' says the south bridge got a new bent — a whole transverse frame — without saying how many bents it had, so nothing is concluded about its span or its pier count. THE SIGNATORIES ARE THE TOWN: G. W. Dole, of Newberry & Dole on South Water Street, and John Miller, signing 'By order of [the Trustees] of the Town of Chicago' — the corporation's first documented public works in this corpus.

The head of the notice is cut ('Boer rane Lot No, 12') and the reading 'Water Lot' is taken from the cleaner printing of the same notice at 1834-02-11 (c008 there), which sets it as '[Wa]ter Lot No. 12'. claims.notes: THIS RESOLVES A NAMED UNREAD IN THE JANUARY PASS. T-0310 read this same standing notice at 1834-01-14 (c003 there) and could take neither the mill's name nor the subscriber's off the page: the print gave 'the Stoner Sere Mil' and 'K IBLE, Sen.', and the ticket's note says explicitly that the difference between a steam mill and a water mill 'matters — a steam mill and a water mill are different buildings — so it stays inside [uncertain: …]'. Four weeks on, the same advertisement prints clean: it is the STEAM SAW MILL and the subscriber is MARK NOBLE, SEN. The issue of 1834-02-11 sets both again identically (c006 there), so the reading has two independent witnesses inside one month and is not a single lucky impression. What the corpus now holds is a steam-powered saw mill standing on the west half of the south-west quarter of section 4, T39N R14E — up the North Branch, north of the platted town — in a town whose buildings are being framed out of sawn lumber, and the man who owned the ground. The dateline still prints '1833' for a notice about 8 January that runs through February 1834, and is read 1834.

Breed has 'sold out his entire Stock of Goods' and is going to New-York as soon as his accounts are settled. Under the epic's ruling 3 a storefront documented in February 1834 stands in the 1835 town unless a claim contradicts it — THIS IS THAT CONTRADICTION, made in advance, and it is why the run was worth making at the level of the individual notice. Breed does not vanish from the town in the same breath: he is still advertising for 'two or three journeymen' in the issue of 1834-02-11, so what closed is the shop and not the man. A. O. T. Breed also stands in the 1 January letter list reprinted in this issue (claim c016), which corroborates him as a resident independently of his own advertisement.

claims.notes: A TENANCY CHAIN ON A TAVERN — 'that noted Tavern Stand in Chicago, lately occupied by Mr. H. W. Wattles'. The building outlasts its keeper and the paper identifies it by the last man in it, which is precisely the naming habit T-0076 asks the records to reproduce. The house is being run as the Traveller's Home by the new subscriber, who does not sign. THE KEEPER'S NAME IS NOT READ FROM FEBRUARY AT ALL. This printing gives 'Mr, Hin. Watihs' and 1834-02-11 gives 'Mr. Hs W, Wattles', which between them fix the surname and nothing else; T-0310 read the same standing advertisement at 1834-01-28 (c009 there) as 'Mr. [Jo]hn W. February's contribution is that the notice is still running — the tavern is under its second keeper continuously from October 1833 to at least 25 February 1834. NO SITE IS GIVEN and the stand is not identified with any of the town's other named taverns — the Eagle, the Green Tree, Graves' or the Chicago Hotel — because nothing here supports that and a wrong identification would put a documented name on the wrong footprint.

claims.notes: THE 1 JANUARY 1834 CHICAGO LETTER LIST, IN ITS THIRD PRINTING, AND THIS IS THE BEST WITNESS TO IT THAT THE CORPUS HOLDS. The list ran on 1834-01-14 (T-0310 c004, cut to a handful of names by W. Kimball's advertisement), on 1834-01-28 (T-0310 c001, where 97 names were minted), and here on 1834-02-04. THE NAMES ARE NOT MINTED AGAIN. T-0292 settled the rule for a list printed more than once — mint it ONCE, from one witness, and record the other printings as reprints — and T-0299 is the open ticket about what happens when that rule is broken: three printings of the July 1834 list put 298 people into the gazetteer three times over, because the identity policy correctly keys on the whole normalized name and 'Anthony Becra' here is 'Anthony Heere' in the January reading. Minting these seventy-one would add seventy-one more of exactly that. So the reading is made in full, in `normalized`, where it is checkable and citable, and the gazetteer is left alone. WHAT THE READING SHOWS IS WORTH THE PASS ANYWAY. The count is stated against the printing: SEVENTY-ONE names survive at name level in the first alphabetical column, running A to H — Atkins to Harkness — with four further lines of the same column reduced to debris ('Mics ierve Otet', 'pestil ponlent 7 ie rcedect Gponeas ACT', 're Pp. ode rear', ''omero''), so the printed first column was about seventy-five names. T-0310 minted NINETY-SEVEN names from the whole list. Seventy-five in the A-H half alone means the printed list was very substantially longer than ninety-seven, and T-0310's own coverage note calling ninety-seven 'a FLOOR and not the printed length' is confirmed by a second witness rather than left as an inference. IT ALSO REFUTES T-0318'S PREMISE. That ticket says the January printings 'do not repair each other and the images are the only route' — it was written without this third printing, which is in the ruled dialect, sets one name per line, and repairs the A-H half at the transcription without any page image at all. Three of T-0318's four cut surnames are legible here: 'William Cr[…]' is WILLIAM CRISS, 'Benj. Cl[…]' reads Benj. Chapman on this impression, and 'Gustavus C[…]' has no counterpart in this column. That is a finding for T-0318 and not a repair made here: repairing it means declaring merges in identity.json with merge_rules, which is that ticket's work and not this one's. A new ticket records it.

claims.notes: A SECOND LETTER LIST IN THE SAME ISSUE, AND IT IS NOT CHICAGO'S — the postmaster signing is Thomas Calaher and not John S. C. Hogan, and the office name is cut after 'Benne'. It is recorded and not minted, exactly as T-0292 recorded the Hennepin, Du Page and Plainfield lists that ran under the Chicago one in October 1834: an out-of-county list names people who were not necessarily in this town and ruling 1 mints residents of Chicago. It is claimed rather than passed over because the epic's letter-list clause is met by SHOWING what was swept, and a list a pass looked at and set aside is evidence, while a list nobody mentions is a hole. The names are given as they can be read for whoever later identifies the office; the segmenter column is the right-hand sliver of the page and every entry is cut at the head.
